question: When coding agents design methods for open-ended AI tasks, how often do they reach the human performance frontier, and are their algorithmic designs genuinely outside the space of human methods or mostly reuse and recombination?

key_findings.claim: Current agents occasionally reach the collected human frontier, but success is concentrated in a few tasks and does not generalize across agents.
key_findings.evidence: Of 72 agent-task-reference configurations, 10 meet or exceed human SOTA, but only on 3 of 6 tasks: eight on GoEmotions and one each on CUB200 and Weather. No agent reaches SOTA on more than two tasks under either reference condition. Human SOTA has the best mean task rank at 2.67; the strongest agent configuration, Gemini CLI with prepared references, is 4.83.

key_findings.claim: Almost all agent methods can be represented inside a design space built from human methods, and nearly half exactly reproduce an observed human algorithmic coordinate.
key_findings.evidence: Only 3.2% of methods are outside the constructed spaces, so 96.8% are in space. Among all methods, 45.3% have Hamming distance zero to a collected human method and another 28.4% differ in one module, placing 73.7% within distance one. Within represented methods, 95.3% of module choices reuse human-observed values and only 4.7% require a new value.

key_findings.claim: Agents explore a narrow subset of available algorithmic coordinates despite receiving budgets for iterative experimentation.
key_findings.evidence: Each configuration may submit up to ten successive solutions, yet the median configuration visits only 3.5 distinct algorithmic coordinates. The five most frequent coordinates account for more than half of all agent methods in four of six tasks and 59.7% on average.

key_findings.claim: Frontier-reaching solutions mostly remain close to human designs and uniformly use ensemble prediction in this sample.
key_findings.evidence: None of 23 out-of-space solutions ranks in its task's top performance quartile. Eight of the 10 SOTA-reaching configurations produce their best SOTA-reaching method within distance two of a human method, 88.0% of those methods' module choices are human-observed, and every best method in the 10 configurations uses an ensemble.

key_findings.claim: Prepared papers and code do not yield a clear performance advantage because agents rarely consult the available human knowledge.
key_findings.evidence: Across 36 matched reference/no-reference comparisons, references improve 20, reduce 15, and leave 1 unchanged; five SOTA-reaching configurations use references and five do not. Internet-enabled agents conduct task-specific searches in only 2 of 60 configurations, access 5.4% of provided references, and consult a top-three reference in only 8 of 36 reference-enabled configurations.

method.core_idea: Represent human and agent methods as coordinates in task-specific modular design spaces so algorithmic differences can be measured independently of source-code or prose similarity.
method.mechanism: For each of six open-ended tasks, agents summarize 327 human reference methods from code, infer a directed acyclic graph of algorithmic modules and observed choices, and iterate with domain experts until the design space is accepted. Human and agent code is mapped into coordinates; the distance between two methods is the number of modules with different choices, and distance to the human set is the minimum such Hamming distance. Six agents then receive up to 24 GPU-hours and ten solution attempts per task, with and without prepared references; task evaluators return only a scalar score.
assumptions: The collected human references cover enough of each task's algorithmic history for distance to that set to be meaningful.
Human-reviewed modules preserve core algorithmic choices while safely abstracting hyperparameters and implementation details.
Every module difference should contribute equally to Hamming distance despite potentially different scientific importance.
The best collected leaderboard score is a useful human frontier even when compute, tuning, and publication conditions differ from the agent budget.
Six tasks across vision, NLP, graphs, and time series are broad enough to expose recurring agent research patterns.

techniques.role: Builds a task-specific graph of modules, dependencies, and observed choices from human paper implementations.
Uses domain experts to correct module boundaries, dependencies, and systematic mapping errors before analysis.
Maps heterogeneous implementations to explicit module choices so semantic design can be compared without textual similarity.
Counts how many modules an agent method changes relative to its closest collected human coordinate.
Separates methods needing a new value in an existing module from methods that require a genuinely new module structure.
Runs each agent-task pair with and without prepared human papers and code while leaving Internet access unchanged.
Allows up to ten code-and-evaluation cycles under a fixed 24-hour, one-V100 budget without revealing test labels.

evaluations.setting: Six agents x six tasks x two reference conditions, 72 configurations
evaluations.metric: Configurations meeting or exceeding collected human SOTA
evaluations.result: 10 of 72 configurations, covering only 3 of 6 tasks
evaluations.baseline: Human SOTA; eight successes are on GoEmotions, one on CUB200, one on Weather

evaluations.setting: All mapped agent methods across six tasks
evaluations.metric: Minimum module-Hamming distance to a collected human method
evaluations.result: 45.3% at distance 0; 28.4% at distance 1; 73.7% at distance at most 1
evaluations.baseline: 3.2% are outside the human-derived design-space structure

evaluations.setting: Methods represented within the constructed design spaces
evaluations.metric: Share of module choices using human-observed values

evaluations.setting: Per-configuration iterative search, at most 10 solutions
evaluations.result: Median 3.5; top five coordinates hold 59.7% of methods on average
evaluations.baseline: The available task design spaces contain many more human-derived combinations

evaluations.metric: Distance and module provenance of their best methods
evaluations.result: 8 of 10 within distance 2; 88.0% of module choices human-observed; 10 of 10 use ensembles
evaluations.baseline: No SOTA-reaching method is out of space

evaluations.setting: Thirty-six paired with-reference versus without-reference configurations
evaluations.baseline: Five SOTA-reaching configurations in each reference condition

limitations: Reviewer-identified: each agent-task-reference cell appears to be one run, so model randomness, agent trajectory variance, and evaluator noise are not estimated.

Reviewer-identified: the six tasks are standard supervised prediction problems with fixed datasets and scalar metrics; they do not represent the full range of scientific discovery, theory, data creation, or environment design.
Reviewer-identified: design spaces are constructed from collected references, not all human work, so missing papers can make established choices look new or make a method appear out of space.
Reviewer-identified: human experts inspect samples and correct systematic errors, but the paper does not report mapping inter-rater reliability or a blinded validation set.

Reviewer-identified: equal-weight Hamming distance ignores whether a changed module is a central algorithmic idea or a minor component; coordinate-preserving hyperparameter innovation is also intentionally invisible.
Reviewer-identified: human SOTA and agent methods are not compute-matched, and agent results select the best of up to ten attempts, complicating direct performance interpretation.

Reviewer-identified: prepared references remain available but mostly unread, so the paired condition tests the combination of provision and agent retrieval policy rather than the value of human knowledge when actually consumed.
failure_modes: A coarse module taxonomy can collapse scientifically distinct methods into one coordinate and overstate imitation.
An overly fine taxonomy can count implementation details as innovation and inflate distance.
Incomplete human reference coverage can misclassify rediscovered prior art as a new module value or out-of-space method.
Agents can overfit scalar evaluator feedback through ensembling or tuning without developing a transferable method.
Providing papers has no effect when the agent does not retrieve, read, or integrate them into experiments.
Repeatedly selecting familiar coordinates can produce local performance gains while leaving genuine space expansion unexplored.
Out-of-space attempts may fail because they are genuinely weak or because a 24-hour one-GPU budget is insufficient to debug unfamiliar designs.
reusable_insights: Evaluate research agents on two axes—task value and algorithmic difference—rather than treating benchmark score as evidence of innovation.
Use code and data flow as the primary evidence for method comparison; prose similarity is a poor proxy for algorithm identity.
Separate new values inside known modules from new module structures; these represent different degrees of design-space expansion.
Track coordinate coverage across an agent's iterations to distinguish real exploration from repeated hyperparameter variations around one design.
Reference access must be paired with retrieval and usage telemetry; availability alone does not measure knowledge integration.
Within-space recombination is a plausible near-term target because it offers more upside than coordinate-preserving tuning and lower risk than unconstrained space expansion.
open_questions: Can a benchmark reward design-space coverage and information gain without encouraging arbitrary novelty that harms performance?
Would retrieval policies that require agents to map and cite relevant prior methods before experimentation improve both novelty assessment and task performance?
How stable are algorithmic coordinates across independent expert panels and alternative module granularities?
Do agent methods remain close to human designs on theorem discovery, RL environment design, data curation, or open-ended science tasks without fixed supervised metrics?
Can agents deliberately pursue space-expanding hypotheses and allocate extra debugging budget when early scalar scores are poor?
How much apparent coordinate reuse comes from pretraining memorization versus rational rediscovery under the task constraints?

competitive_landscape.title: InnoGym: Benchmarking the Innovation Potential of AI Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: InnoGym jointly scores performance gain and methodological novelty across 18 engineering and science tasks, with novelty judged by model comparisons. This paper uses explicit human-derived module coordinates and expert-reviewed code mappings, trading broader task coverage for traceable structural differences and less dependence on an LLM judge.

competitive_landscape.title: MLGym: A New Framework and Benchmark for Advancing AI Research Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: MLGym provides 13 open-ended research environments and observes that agents mainly improve hyperparameters rather than inventing hypotheses or architectures. This paper operationalizes that qualitative observation by mapping methods to modular design coordinates and measuring distance, reuse, and exploration concentration.

competitive_landscape.title: MLAgentBench: Evaluating Language Agents on Machine Learning Experimentation
competitive_landscape.difference: MLAgentBench measures experimentation success, plans, and actions on 13 ML tasks. This paper adds human SOTA leaderboards, a paired reference condition, and algorithm-level representation to ask what kind of method produced the score.

competitive_landscape.title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
competitive_landscape.difference: MLE-bench uses 75 Kaggle competitions and medal thresholds to assess engineering performance and resource scaling. This paper uses only six tasks but collects paper-and-code lineages and quantifies whether solutions reproduce, recombine, or extend human method structures.

competitive_landscape.title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
competitive_landscape.difference: The AI Scientist automates idea generation through paper writing and uses an automated reviewer to estimate novelty and acceptance. This work narrows evaluation to runnable task methods and replaces prose/reviewer novelty with expert-reviewed module coordinates grounded in code.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is a systematic empirical study of both performance and algorithmic design for widely used agents, using explicit human-derived design spaces rather than an opaque novelty judge. Primary benchmarks already show that research agents can improve ML tasks and often favor familiar tuning, while InnoGym explicitly evaluates methodological novelty. Reviewer inference: the distinctive contribution is the auditable coordinate representation and its quantitative evidence of narrow exploration, not the broader claim that agents imitate existing work. The 96.8% in-space result is informative but taxonomy-dependent, and the lack of repeated agent runs or mapping reliability estimates prevents treating the exact percentages as universal constants.
reviewer_notes: Quantitative claims were checked against pages 5-7, especially Table 2 and Figures 3-5. 'Human SOTA' means the best collected leaderboard entry, not a compute-matched human trial. Competitive methods and identifiers were verified on primary arXiv records.
